narrativeProgression.description: The interviewer asks Chris Abele about his feelings on early election results.
Chris Abele expresses his positive feelings and notes the high voter turnout.
He discusses Obama's likely victory margin in the state.
Chris Abele reflects on past elections and the importance of voter turnout in Wisconsin.
He humorously comments on the frequency of elections in Wisconsin.
Chris Abele expresses his hope for a less politically charged environment after the election.
The interviewer asks about the impact of Obama's presidency on Chris Abele personally.
Chris Abele discusses the impact of federally funded programs and the differences in perspective between Obama and Governor Romney.
He highlights the potential for significant adjustments for the county based on the election results.
Chris Abele expresses his hope for minimal adaptation depending on the outcome.
The interviewer asks for his perspective as a taxpayer and resident.
Chris Abele notes his relief at the end of the campaign season.
He describes his political and social leanings and his positive working relationships with both Democratic and Republican leaders.
Chris Abele emphasizes the need for more agreement and collaboration in politics.
He laments the focus on fringe issues in political discourse.
Chris Abele emphasizes the need to focus on common ground and work together.
He expresses his pride in his country, state, and county.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: So we've had a few states announced so far. How are you feeling? You feel pretty good about this?
Yeah, I feel very good about this. I mean, it'll be interesting to see, but so far, it looks like the turnout is huge everywhere.
I think the margin looks like in this state for Obama is pretty solid, which is, you know, as we all remember what happened a couple of years ago.
But what's fascinating to me is this state, verenially, you know, highest voter turnout in the country.
I mean, we do a lot of voting and we hear ourselves a lot of practice clearly because we have elections every 10 seconds.
But all that aside, how about everybody is looking forward to tomorrow, and not seeing every 10 seconds on TV who they should be angry at, and can start getting along with each other.
But yet, tonight, I'm happy about how things are turning out.
My last question, I've been asking a lot of voters, particularly, that even yourself isn't running executive.
How has Obama's presidency impacted you personally?
Sure. Well, I mean, from the point of view of the counties, since when all counties do, there's a lot of federally funded programs.
And there's some very different views between President Obama and Governor Romney and how they view some of the programs that directly impact counties.
So there would be significant adapting on our part, to have to do.
But it's needless to say, I'm hoping not to have to adapt too much.
And how about you just add a taxpayer as a resident, as just an everyday news?
Well, sure. You know, I'll tell you one thing. The other reason I'll be glad to be on the other end of campaign season is politically.
Basically, I'm pretty concerned. And so, see, I'm really a liberal. I have a great relationship with Mayor Marrett.
I've got a good relationship with Governor Walker. And to me, I really think more people can agree on those things that are new.
And we spend so much time talking about the fringes of times, what we disagree as. And then on what we do, we're just both of everything that we agree on.
And it's a lot easier and getting done when we see what we agree on and work out.
And we all live in the greatest country in the world. I happen to think that we live in the greatest state in the world and the greatest county in the world.
And that, we can all agree on.
